summary: When God surveys all he has made, he calls it very good. The same word that intensifies “good” can carry a personal ending: Israel is to love Yahweh with all its might, and Josiah turns to him with all his might.

senses.definition: Used adverbially, it gives the degree of a quality or action. Repetition can heighten it further.

evidence.note: The good of the preceding days (Gen 1:25) becomes very good when God sees the whole.
The doubled word describes how greatly the waters rose.

senses.definition: With a possessive ending it names the might a person brings to an act of devotion. Josiah's response to the law echoes the command given to Israel.

evidence.note: With all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.
Josiah turned to Yahweh with all his heart, soul and might according to the law of Moses.
Jesus includes all one's strength when citing the command.
The letter uses it to intensify strength. In the poem the mountains bring plenty of silver.

evidence.locator: armep x000012400, mādiš (adverb); compare armep x000004720, mādu (adjective)
evidence.note: The glossary records maʾdiš alongside mādiš. The adjective maʾdu describes what is abundant or numerous.

note: Does the possessive use distinguish strength from the resources a person commands? The two Hebrew passages do not enumerate these. Lane, p. 2687, n38182, Arabic maʾada describes a flourishing, supple plant; its relationship to the Hebrew intensifier is uncertain. The proposed Sabaean parallel still needs a securely located inscription.
